Alain Resnais. A French filmmaker whose obsession with memory, narrative structure, and the gap between word and image created some of cinema's most formally sophisticated and philosophically dense works. Beginning with documentaries, he moved into features that fragmented causality and chronology, exploring how the mind reconstructs the past and constructs identity.

He directed Hiroshima Mon Amour in 1959, a rhapsodic meditation on memory and love between a French woman and a Japanese man, interweaving atomic-bomb testimony with romantic narrative. He made Last Year at Marienbad in 1961, a puzzle-box narrative where past and present collapse. A man insists a woman promised to run away with him at a resort, though she denies any memory of him, and reality becomes ambiguous. He began his career with documentary shorts, including Night and Fog in 1955, a devastating essay on the Holocaust using archival footage and contemporary images.

Resnais pioneered the use of voice-over as a second narrative layer, with characters' thoughts and memories inhabiting the soundtrack while images occupy the screen. He collaborated with writers Alain Robbe-Grillet and Marguerite Duras, adapting the nouveau roman's foregrounding of style and the instability of narrative itself. Rather than composing films using plot, he used visual rhyming and symphonic structure, seeing film as music rather than literature. His later work integrated musical theatre and modernist techniques, and he remained formally adventurous until his death at ninety-one.

Marguerite Duras was his writer and collaborator on Hiroshima Mon Amour, her poetic approach to language and time shaping his narrative philosophy. He shares with Jean-Luc Godard the role of contemporary formalist, though where both questioned narrative convention, Resnais retained more lyricism. His work was influenced by the nouveau roman literary movement and its instability of memory. He was a contemporary explorer with Agnès Varda of subjective time and fragmented narrative.
